Two hues opposite each other on the wheel. Maximum contrast and energy — use one as dominant and the other sparingly as an accent.
Three neighbors on the wheel. Calm and cohesive — pick one to dominate so the scheme doesn\'t wash out.
Three hues 120° apart. Vibrant yet balanced — let one color lead and mute the other two.
A base plus the two neighbors of its complement. Nearly as much contrast as complementary, with less visual tension.
Two complementary pairs (90° apart). The richest scheme — it only works when one color clearly dominates.
A single hue in multiple tints and shades. Effortlessly elegant — differentiate with lightness, not hue.

WCAG 2.1 thresholds — body text: 4.5:1 (AA), 7:1 (AAA). Large text (≥18pt bold or 24pt): 3:1. UI components and icons: 3:1 against adjacent colors.
APCA is the perceptual model proposed for WCAG 3 — it accounts for polarity and screen rendering better than the 2.x ratio. Values ≥ 75 Lc suit body text; ≥ 60 works for larger text.
Every tonal color as text (rows) on every tonal color as background (columns). Watch the pass/fail frontier hug the diagonal — similar lightness never reads.
Same tone = 1:1 — the diagonal is always unreadable.

Rows choose the text color, columns the background. Only pairs far apart in lightness pass — which is exactly why design systems reserve dark tones for text on light surfaces and never place body text on similarly lit containers.

resources.string: Tap a swatch to make it the builder base and generate a tonal scale from it.
What most tools do — fast, but midpoints go dark and muddy.
Physically correct light mixing — midpoints stay bright.
Perceptually uniform — the smoothest, most even ramp.

Blending in sRGB averages the stored numbers, so midpoints skew dark and muddy. Linear-light blending is physically correct. OKLab blending is perceptually even — watch the mid swatch jump between modes; that jump is the banding you\'d ship.
Every Material 3 app starts from one seed color. Watch a single hue become a full scheme — with every readable pair verified by the same WCAG math from lesson 6.
If any pair fell below 4.5:1, the generator already nudged its lightness — this list is proof, not decoration.
Copy Compose light + dark theme code
Compose theme copied — paste it into your ui/theme

How it works: the seed becomes an OKLCH hue. Five tonal palettes are built (vivid primary, muted secondary, hue-rotated tertiary, near-neutral surface and variant), roles pick tones following Material 3\'s lightness relationships, and chroma is gamut-mapped — never clipped — so hue survives.
Applied — this app now runs your scheme
Same two ingredients, two different physics. Screens ADD light (lesson: RGB). Pigments REMOVE it — each layer filters what the next can reflect.

• Additive: more light → brighter. Complementary lights sum to white.\n• Subtractive: more pigment → darker. Complementary filters cancel to black.\n• This is why print uses CMY and screens use RGB — same wheel, opposite mixing rules.
Lesson 4 said the same color changes with its neighbors. Don\'t take the lesson\'s word for it — drive it yourself.
The left gray looked lighter sitting on the dark surround, the right one darker on the light surround — yet neither moved. Your visual system reports contrast, not absolute values.

This is exactly why the Contrast checker exists: never judge a color in isolation, and never trust \"it looks fine\" — measure it. Try copying the center color into the checker against both surrounds and watch the ratio barely move while your perception swings.
About 8% of men and 0.5% of women perceive color differently. Design that relies on hue alone excludes them.
